title: Intertemporal Equilibrium with Knowledge Production
text:
The basic mechanism of the model is closely related to the R&D-based growth literature. Romer (1990) treats technological change as the outcome of intentional R&D investment and emphasizes the allocation of productive resources to research, while Jones (1995) considers a more general knowledge-production process in which the creation of new knowledge may depend on both R&D inputs and the existing stock of knowledge. The linear additive R&D specification adopted here can be viewed as a simple special case in which the increment in the production-efficiency parameter is proportional to current R&D labor and independent of the existing level of technology.
Assume the following:

The economy has \(n_p\) periods. A firm operating in period \(t\) starts production at the beginning of the period and obtains its product at the end of period \(t\), or equivalently at the beginning of period \(t+1\). Hence there are \(n_p-1\) interperiod production activities. In general, an \(n_p\)-period model may contain \(n_p\) dated products, but in the present example the initial-period product supply and consumption are omitted. The product commodities are therefore \(product^{(2)},\ldots,product^{(n_p)}\).
The economy contains four types of dated commodities: products, labor, technology knowledge (i.e., production-efficiency parameters), and scale claims. Product firms operate in periods \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-1\), R&D firms operate in periods \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-2\), and there is one intertemporal consumer. Commodities dated at different periods are treated as different commodities.
The product firm operating in period \(t\) uses the production-efficiency parameter \(\alpha^{(t)}\) and production labor \(x^{(t)}\) to produce the product available in period \(t+1\) according to \(c^{(t+1)}=\alpha^{(t)}x^{(t)}\). To represent this technology as a degree-one homogeneous production function, a scale claim \(c_s^{(t)}\) is introduced, giving

\[
g\left(\alpha^{(t)},x^{(t)},c_s^{(t)}\right)
=
\frac{\alpha^{(t)}x^{(t)}}{c_s^{(t)}}
\]
The product firm follows the marginal pricing principle.

The R&D firm operating in period \(t\) uses R&D labor \(\ell^{(t)}\) to increase production efficiency from period \(t+1\) onward. With R&D-efficiency parameter \(\bar\alpha>0\), one unit of R&D labor generates \(\bar\alpha\) units of each future production-efficiency parameter commodity (i.e., technology knowledge) within the production horizon. Hence \(\alpha^{(t+1)}=\alpha^{(t)}+\bar\alpha\ell^{(t)}\) for \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-2\), or equivalently

\[
\alpha^{(t)}
=
\alpha^{(1)}
+
\bar\alpha
\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\ell^{(s)},
\qquad
t=2,\ldots,n_p-1
\]

The consumer is endowed with \(\omega>0\) units of labor and one unit of the scale claim in each production period, together with \(\alpha^{(1)}\) units of each dated production-efficiency parameter commodity. Labor-market balance is \(x^{(t)}+\ell^{(t)}=\omega\) for \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-2\), while \(x^{(n_p-1)}=\omega\) because R&D in the last production period cannot affect production within the horizon.
The consumer consumes \(c^{(2)},\ldots,c^{(n_p)}\) and has intertemporal utility

\[
u
=
\sum_{t=2}^{n_p}\rho^t\ln c^{(t)},
\qquad
0<\rho<1
\]
For the infinite-horizon version of the model, the critical production-efficiency level for R&D is
\[
\alpha^*
=
\frac{\rho\bar\alpha\omega}{1-\rho}
\tag{1}\]
R&D is undertaken when \(\alpha^{(t)}<\alpha^*\) and ceases once the production-efficiency parameter reaches the critical level. In particular, if \(\alpha^{(1)}\geq\alpha^*\), there is no incentive to undertake R&D.
The finite horizon generates a terminal effect. R&D undertaken late in the horizon affects fewer future production periods, so the incentive to undertake R&D declines near the terminal period and eventually disappears.
For \(n_p=9\), \(\rho=0.8\), \(\alpha^{(1)}=0.01\), \(\bar\alpha=0.0001\), and \(\omega=100\), the equilibrium R&D-labor path is approximately \((43.02,33.09,23.10,10.99,0,0,0)\). The corresponding productivity increments \(\bar\alpha\ell^{(t)}\) are approximately \((0.004302,0.003309,0.002310,0.001099,0,0,0)\). The resulting productivity path is
\[
\left(
\alpha^{(2)},\ldots,\alpha^{(8)}
\right)
=
\left(
0.01430,\,
0.01761,\,
0.01992,\,
0.02102,\,
0.02102,\,
0.02102,\,
0.02102
\right)
\]
Thus positive R&D occurs only in the first four R&D periods.



Listing 1: A \(4\times3\) Technology-Accumulation Intertemporal Equilibrium Model with Additive R&D


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEMB
using Plots

np = 9

rho = 0.8
alpha1 = 0.01
alpha_bar = 0.0001
omega = 100.0

np >= 3 || throw(ArgumentError("np must be at least 3."))

product(t) = CommodityRef(:product; period=t)
labor(t) = CommodityRef(:labor; period=t)
parameter(t) = CommodityRef(:parameter; period=t)
scale_claim(t) = CommodityRef(:scale_claim; period=t)

alpha_star =
    rho * alpha_bar * omega / (1 - rho)

alpha_target_start = if alpha1 < alpha_star
    alpha_star .-
    (alpha_star - alpha1) .* rho .^ (0:(np - 2))
else
    fill(alpha1, np - 1)
end

research_labor_start = clamp.(
    diff(alpha_target_start) ./ alpha_bar,
    0.0,
    0.9 * omega,
)

alpha_start =
    alpha1 .+
    alpha_bar .* vcat(
        0.0,
        cumsum(research_labor_start),
    )

production_labor_start =
    vcat(
        omega .- research_labor_start,
        omega,
    )

product_start =
    alpha_start .* production_labor_start

product_p0 = [
    rho^(t - 2) *
    product_start[1] /
    product_start[t - 1]
    for t in 2:np
]

labor_p0 =
    product_p0 .* alpha_start

parameter_p0 =
    product_p0 .* production_labor_start

scale_claim_p0 =
    -product_p0 .* product_start

p0 = vcat(
    product_p0,
    labor_p0,
    parameter_p0,
    scale_claim_p0,
)

production_function = inputs -> begin
    a, x, cs = inputs
    a * x / cs
end

marginal_product_function = inputs -> begin
    a, x, cs = inputs
    [x * cs, a * cs, -a * x]
end

production_spec = ProductionFunctionSpec(
    production_function,
    marginal_product_function;
    behavior=:stationary,
)

research_spec = ActivityDemandSpec(
    (activity, prices) -> [
        activity,
    ],
)

model = GEMBModel(
    [
        CommoditySpec(
            :product;
            axes=(period=2:np,),
            price_lower_bound=0.0,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :labor;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=0.0,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :parameter;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=0.0,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :scale_claim;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=-Inf,
        ),
    ];
    numeraire=product(2),
)

for t in 1:(np - 1)
    add_agent!(
        model,
        production_spec;
        outputs=product(t + 1),
        demands=[
            parameter(t),
            labor(t),
            scale_claim(t),
        ],
        activity_start=product_start[t],
        demand_start=[
            alpha_start[t],
            production_labor_start[t],
            1.0,
        ],
        demand_lower_bounds=[
            1.0e-12,
            1.0e-12,
            1.0e-12,
        ],
        production_multiplier_start=product_p0[t],
        name=Symbol("production_$t"),
    )
end

for t in 1:(np - 2)
    add_agent!(
        model,
        research_spec;
        outputs=[
            parameter(s)
            for s in (t + 1):(np - 1)
        ],
        output_coefficients=fill(
            alpha_bar,
            np - t - 1,
        ),
        demands=labor(t),
        activity_start=research_labor_start[t],
        activity_lower_bound=0.0,
        activity_upper_bound=omega,
        name=Symbol("research_$t"),
    )
end

utility_weights =
    rho .^ (2:np)

add_agent!(
    model,
    CESMarginalUtilitySpec(
        utility_weights;
        es=1.0,
    );
    demands=CommodityRef(:product),
    endowments=[
        CommodityRef(:labor),
        CommodityRef(:parameter),
        CommodityRef(:scale_claim),
    ],
    endowment_quantities=vcat(
        fill(omega, np - 1),
        fill(alpha1, np - 1),
        fill(1.0, np - 1),
    ),
    demand_start=product_start,
    demand_lower_bounds=fill(
        1.0e-12,
        np - 1,
    ),
    multiplier_start=
        rho^2 / product_start[1],
    multiplier_lower_bound=0.0,
    name=:consumer,
)

result = solve(
    model;
    p0=p0,
    residual_tol=1.0e-9,
    silent=true,
)

result.solved || error("Equilibrium solve failed.")

stats = equilibrium_statistics(model, result)
print_equilibrium_statistics(model, result)

research_labor =
    stats.activity_levels[np:(2 * np - 3)]

alpha_path =
    alpha1 .+
    alpha_bar .* cumsum(research_labor)

display(
    plot(
        2:(np - 1),
        alpha_path;
        xlabel="Period",
        ylabel="alpha^(t)",
        label="alpha^(t)",
        legend=:bottomright,
        marker=:circle,
        grid=true,
        gridalpha=1.0,
    ),
)






The same economy can also be represented as a general equilibrium model in which production-efficiency parameters are treated as tradable parameter commodities. The period convention is the same as in the technology-accumulation intertemporal equilibrium model: \(n_p\) denotes the number of periods, production occurs in periods \(1,\ldots,n_p-1\), and the product produced in period \(t\) becomes available in period \(t+1\).
Since \(c^{(t+1)}=\alpha^{(t)}x^{(t)}\), the intertemporal utility can be written as
\[
u
=
\sum_{t=1}^{n_p-1}
\rho^{t+1}
\left(
\ln\alpha^{(t)}
+
\ln x^{(t)}
\right)
\]
Because \(\alpha^{(1)}\) is given and \(x^{(n_p-1)}=\omega\), their contributions to utility are constant and can be omitted. The resulting reduced-form utility is
\[
U
=
\sum_{t=2}^{n_p-1}
\rho^{t+1}\ln\alpha^{(t)}
+
\sum_{t=1}^{n_p-2}
\rho^{t+1}\ln x^{(t)}
\]
The dated product commodities and the corresponding production firms can therefore be eliminated from the reduced-form model. The reduced economy contains \(n_p-2\) dated technology commodities, \(technology^{(2)},\ldots,technology^{(n_p-1)}\), and \(n_p-2\) dated labor commodities, \(labor^{(1)},\ldots,labor^{(n_p-2)}\). The consumer is endowed with \(\alpha^{(1)}\) units of each technology knowledge and \(\omega\) units of each labor commodity.
Let \(\ell^{(t)}\) denote the activity level of the R&D firm operating in period \(t\). The activity level directly measures the amount of labor allocated to R&D in that period. One unit of R&D activity requires one unit of period-\(t\) labor and jointly produces \(\bar\alpha\) units of each future technology knowledge dated from period \(t+1\) through period \(n_p-1\).
The two equilibrium models use different commodity and agent structures but generate the same R&D-labor allocation, production-labor allocation, and productivity path. The final-product quantities in the technology-accumulation intertemporal equilibrium model can be recovered from \(c^{(t+1)}=\alpha^{(t)}x^{(t)}\).



Listing 2: A \(2\times2\) Technology-Trade General Equilibrium Model with Additive R&D


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEMB
using Plots

np = 9

rho = 0.8
alpha1 = 0.01
alpha_bar = 0.0001
omega = 100.0

np >= 3 || throw(ArgumentError("np must be at least 3."))

nt = np - 2

technology(t) = CommodityRef(:technology; period=t)
labor(t) = CommodityRef(:labor; period=t)

utility_weights = vcat(
    rho .^ (3:np),
    rho .^ (2:(np - 1)),
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Starting values
# ------------------------------------------------------------

alpha_star =
    rho * alpha_bar * omega / (1 - rho)

alpha_target_start = if alpha1 < alpha_star
    alpha_star .-
    (alpha_star - alpha1) .* rho .^ (0:(np - 2))
else
    fill(alpha1, np - 1)
end

research_labor_start = clamp.(
    diff(alpha_target_start) ./ alpha_bar,
    0.0,
    0.9 * omega,
)

alpha_start =
    alpha1 .+
    alpha_bar .* vcat(
        0.0,
        cumsum(research_labor_start),
    )

production_labor_start =
    omega .-
    research_labor_start

technology_p0 = [
    rho^(t - 1) *
    production_labor_start[1] /
    alpha_start[t]
    for t in 2:(np - 1)
]

labor_p0 = [
    rho^(t - 1) *
    production_labor_start[1] /
    production_labor_start[t]
    for t in 1:(np - 2)
]

p0 = vcat(
    technology_p0,
    labor_p0,
)

multiplier_start =
    rho^2 / production_labor_start[1]

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Model
# ------------------------------------------------------------

model = GEMBModel(
    [
        CommoditySpec(
            :technology;
            axes=(period=2:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=0.0,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :labor;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 2),),
            price_lower_bound=0.0,
        ),
    ];
    numeraire=labor(1),
)

research_spec = ActivityDemandSpec(
    (activity, prices) -> [
        activity,
    ],
)

for t in 1:(np - 2)
    add_agent!(
        model,
        research_spec;
        outputs=[
            technology(s)
            for s in (t + 1):(np - 1)
        ],
        output_coefficients=fill(
            alpha_bar,
            np - t - 1,
        ),
        demands=labor(t),
        activity_start=research_labor_start[t],
        activity_lower_bound=0.0,
        activity_upper_bound=omega,
        name=Symbol("research_$t"),
    )
end

add_agent!(
    model,
    CESMarginalUtilitySpec(
        utility_weights;
        es=1.0,
    );
    demands=[
        CommodityRef(:technology),
        CommodityRef(:labor),
    ],
    endowments=[
        CommodityRef(:technology),
        CommodityRef(:labor),
    ],
    endowment_quantities=vcat(
        fill(alpha1, nt),
        fill(omega, nt),
    ),
    demand_start=vcat(
        alpha_start[2:end],
        production_labor_start,
    ),
    demand_lower_bounds=fill(
        1.0e-12,
        2 * nt,
    ),
    multiplier_start=multiplier_start,
    multiplier_lower_bound=0.0,
    name=:consumer,
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Solve
# ------------------------------------------------------------

result = solve(
    model;
    p0=p0,
    residual_tol=1.0e-9,
    silent=true,
)

result.solved || error("Equilibrium solve failed.")

stats = equilibrium_statistics(model, result)

print_equilibrium_statistics(model, result)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Technology path
# ------------------------------------------------------------

research_labor = stats.activity_levels

alpha_path =
    alpha1 .+
    alpha_bar .* cumsum(research_labor)

display(
    plot(
        2:(np - 1),
        alpha_path;
        mark=:circle,
        xlabel="Period",
        ylabel="alpha^(t)",
        label="alpha^(t)",
        legend=:bottomright,
        grid=true,
        gridalpha=1.0,
    ),
)

        label="alpha^(t)",
        legend=:bottomright,
        marker=:circle,
        grid=true,
        gridalpha=1.0,
    ),
)






The same economy can also be represented as a general equilibrium model in which production-efficiency parameters are treated as tradable parameter commodities. The period convention is the same as in the technology-accumulation intertemporal equilibrium model: \(n_p\) denotes the number of periods, production occurs in periods \(1,\ldots,n_p-1\), and the product produced in period \(t\) becomes available in period \(t+1\).
Since \(c^{(t+1)}=\alpha^{(t)}x^{(t)}\), the intertemporal utility can be written as
\[
u
=
\sum_{t=1}^{n_p-1}
\rho^{t+1}
\left(
\ln\alpha^{(t)}
+
\ln x^{(t)}
\right)
\]
Because \(\alpha^{(1)}\) is given and \(x^{(n_p-1)}=\omega\), their contributions to utility are constant and can be omitted. The resulting reduced-form utility is
\[
U
=
\sum_{t=2}^{n_p-1}
\rho^{t+1}\ln\alpha^{(t)}
+
\sum_{t=1}^{n_p-2}
\rho^{t+1}\ln x^{(t)}
\]
The dated product commodities and the corresponding production firms can therefore be eliminated from the reduced-form model. The reduced economy contains \(n_p-2\) dated technology commodities, \(technology^{(2)},\ldots,technology^{(n_p-1)}\), and \(n_p-2\) dated labor commodities, \(labor^{(1)},\ldots,labor^{(n_p-2)}\). The consumer is endowed with \(\alpha^{(1)}\) units of each technology knowledge and \(\omega\) units of each labor commodity.
Let \(\ell^{(t)}\) denote the activity level of the R&D firm operating in period \(t\). The activity level directly measures the amount of labor allocated to R&D in that period. One unit of R&D activity requires one unit of period-\(t\) labor and jointly produces \(\bar\alpha\) units of each future technology knowledge dated from period \(t+1\) through period \(n_p-1\).
The two equilibrium models use different commodity and agent structures but generate the same R&D-labor allocation, production-labor allocation, and productivity path. The final-product quantities in the technology-accumulation intertemporal equilibrium model can be recovered from \(c^{(t+1)}=\alpha^{(t)}x^{(t)}\).



Listing 2: A \(2\times2\) Technology-Trade General Equilibrium Model with Additive R&D


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEMB
using Plots

np = 9

rho = 0.8
alpha1 = 0.01
alpha_bar = 0.0001
omega = 100.0

np >= 3 || throw(ArgumentError("np must be at least 3."))

nt = np - 2

technology(t) = CommodityRef(:technology; period=t)
labor(t) = CommodityRef(:labor; period=t)

utility_weights = vcat(
    rho .^ (3:np),
    rho .^ (2:(np - 1)),
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Starting values
# ------------------------------------------------------------

alpha_star =
    rho * alpha_bar * omega / (1 - rho)

alpha_target_start = if alpha1 < alpha_star
    alpha_star .-
    (alpha_star - alpha1) .* rho .^ (0:(np - 2))
else
    fill(alpha1, np - 1)
end

research_labor_start = clamp.(
    diff(alpha_target_start) ./ alpha_bar,
    0.0,
    0.9 * omega,
)

alpha_start =
    alpha1 .+
    alpha_bar .* vcat(
        0.0,
        cumsum(research_labor_start),
    )

production_labor_start =
    omega .-
    research_labor_start

technology_p0 = [
    rho^(t - 1) *
    production_labor_start[1] /
    alpha_start[t]
    for t in 2:(np - 1)
]

labor_p0 = [
    rho^(t - 1) *
    production_labor_start[1] /
    production_labor_start[t]
    for t in 1:(np - 2)
]

p0 = vcat(
    technology_p0,
    labor_p0,
)

multiplier_start =
    rho^2 / production_labor_start[1]

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Model
# ------------------------------------------------------------

model = GEMBModel(
    [
        CommoditySpec(
            :technology;
            axes=(period=2:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=0.0,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :labor;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 2),),
            price_lower_bound=0.0,
        ),
    ];
    numeraire=labor(1),
)

research_spec = ActivityDemandSpec(
    (activity, prices) -> [
        activity,
    ],
)

for t in 1:(np - 2)
    add_agent!(
        model,
        research_spec;
        outputs=[
            technology(s)
            for s in (t + 1):(np - 1)
        ],
        output_coefficients=fill(
            alpha_bar,
            np - t - 1,
        ),
        demands=labor(t),
        activity_start=research_labor_start[t],
        activity_lower_bound=0.0,
        activity_upper_bound=omega,
        name=Symbol("research_$t"),
    )
end

add_agent!(
    model,
    CESMarginalUtilitySpec(
        utility_weights;
        es=1.0,
    );
    demands=[
        CommodityRef(:technology),
        CommodityRef(:labor),
    ],
    endowments=[
        CommodityRef(:technology),
        CommodityRef(:labor),
    ],
    endowment_quantities=vcat(
        fill(alpha1, nt),
        fill(omega, nt),
    ),
    demand_start=vcat(
        alpha_start[2:end],
        production_labor_start,
    ),
    demand_lower_bounds=fill(
        1.0e-12,
        2 * nt,
    ),
    multiplier_start=multiplier_start,
    multiplier_lower_bound=0.0,
    name=:consumer,
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Solve
# ------------------------------------------------------------

result = solve(
    model;
    p0=p0,
    residual_tol=1.0e-9,
    silent=true,
)

result.solved || error("Equilibrium solve failed.")

stats = equilibrium_statistics(model, result)

print_equilibrium_statistics(model, result)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Technology path
# ------------------------------------------------------------

research_labor = stats.activity_levels

alpha_path =
    alpha1 .+
    alpha_bar .* cumsum(research_labor)

display(
    plot(
        2:(np - 1),
        alpha_path;
        mark=:circle,
        xlabel="Period",
        ylabel="alpha^(t)",
        label="alpha^(t)",
        legend=:bottomright,
        grid=true,
        gridalpha=1.0,
    ),
)

title: Intertemporal Equilibrium with Knowledge Production
section: Finite-Horizon Equilibrium with Linear Multiplicative R&D
text:
Finite-Horizon Equilibrium with Linear Multiplicative R&D

Linear Multiplicative R&D
We now modify the model from the previous section by replacing its R&D function.
Consider the multiplicative technology-accumulation equation
\[
\alpha^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha^{(t)}
\left(
1+\bar\alpha\ell^{(t)}
\right)
\]
where \(\ell^{(t)}\) denotes R&D labor in period \(t\). Production in period \(t\) generates the product available in period \(t+1\), so production takes place in periods \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-1\), while useful R&D activities take place only in periods \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-2\). The production relation is
\[
c^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha^{(t)}x^{(t)}
\]
with \(x^{(t)}=\omega-\ell^{(t)}\) for \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-2\) and \(x^{(n_p-1)}=\omega\).


Analytical Solution
For the infinite-horizon model, positive R&D occurs when
\[
\rho(1+\bar\alpha\omega)>1
\]
When this condition holds, the optimal R&D labor input is
\[
\ell^*
=
\rho\omega
-
\frac{1-\rho}{\bar\alpha}
\]
The corresponding productivity path is
\[
\alpha^{(t)}
=
\alpha^{(1)}
\left[
\rho(1+\bar\alpha\omega)
\right]^{t-1},
\qquad
t=1,2,\ldots
\]
For the finite-horizon model, define
\[
q^{(t)}
=
\sum_{k=0}^{n_p-t-1}\rho^k
=
\frac{1-\rho^{n_p-t}}{1-\rho},
\qquad
t=1,\ldots,n_p-2
\]
The optimal R&D labor input is
\[
\ell^{*(t)}
=
\begin{cases}
0,
&
\displaystyle
q^{(t)}
\leq
1+\frac{1}{\bar\alpha\omega}
\\[1em]
\displaystyle
\omega
-
\frac{1}{q^{(t)}}
\left(
\omega+\frac{1}{\bar\alpha}
\right),
&
\displaystyle
q^{(t)}
>
1+\frac{1}{\bar\alpha\omega}
\end{cases}
\]
Thus R&D eventually disappears as the terminal period approaches. When the long-run R&D condition holds, define
\[
k^*
=
\left\lfloor
\frac{
\ln\left(
\rho-\frac{1-\rho}{\bar\alpha\omega}
\right)
}{
\ln\rho
}
\right\rfloor
\]
Provided that \(n_p\geq k^*+2\), the last period with positive R&D is \(n_p-k^*-1\). During periods with positive R&D, productivity evolves according to
\[
\alpha^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha^{(t)}
\rho(1+\bar\alpha\omega)
\frac{q^{(t+1)}}{q^{(t)}}
\]
and remains constant thereafter.



GEMB Implementation of the Multiplicative R&D Model
The GEMB implementation contains six types of dated commodities: product, labor, technology stock, technology service, product scale claim, and research scale claim. There are three types of economic agents: production firms, R&D firms, and a representative consumer. In addition, a terminal technology agent is introduced as a technical device in the final production period.
Several commodity types are introduced specifically for implementing the model. In particular, the technology stock and the technology service used in current production are represented separately. The technology stock available at the beginning of period \(t\) has two roles. It provides the technology service used by the period-\(t\) production firm, and it also serves as the technological base from which the next-period technology stock is generated. Separating these two roles makes it possible to represent explicitly both the current productive use of technology and its intertemporal accumulation.
Two different scale-claim commodities are also introduced. The product scale claim, denoted by \(c_p^{(t)}\), is associated with the production technology, while the research scale claim, denoted by \(c_r^{(t)}\), is associated with the R&D technology. One unit of each corresponding scale claim is supplied in each relevant period, so market clearing gives \(c_p^{(t)}=1\) and \(c_r^{(t)}=1\). These commodities allow the two technologies to be represented in degree-one homogeneous form.
The period-\(t\) production firm uses technology service, labor, and the product scale claim to produce the product available in period \(t+1\). Its homogenized production function is
\[
g(a,x,c_p)
=
\frac{ax}{c_p}
\]
where \(a\) is the technology service and \(x\) is production labor. When \(c_p=1\), this reduces to the original production relation
\[
c^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha^{(t)}x^{(t)}
\]
The production firm can therefore be represented directly by a standard production-function specification with marginal-pricing conditions.
The R&D firm requires a different treatment. Let \(a\), \(\ell\), and \(c_r\) denote its inputs of current technology stock, R&D labor, and research scale claim. The firm supplies \(a\) units of current technology service and produces the next-period technology stock according to
\[
a'
=
a
\left(
1+\bar\alpha\frac{\ell}{c_r}
\right)
\]
This technology is homogeneous of degree one in \((a,\ell,c_r)\). When \(c_r=1\), it becomes
\[
\alpha^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha^{(t)}
\left(
1+\bar\alpha\ell^{(t)}
\right)
\]
and hence
\[
\alpha^{(t+1)}-\alpha^{(t)}
=
\bar\alpha\alpha^{(t)}\ell^{(t)}
\]
The productivity of R&D labor depends on the current technology stock, so one unit of R&D labor does not generate a fixed amount of future technology. The R&D firm cannot therefore be represented directly by an activity-demand specification.
The R&D firm also cannot be represented directly by the standard production-function specification. Although this specification allows joint outputs, their quantities are proportional to a common activity level through fixed output coefficients.
The R&D firm is consequently implemented as an explicit net-supply agent. Over current technology stock, labor, research scale claim, current technology service, and next-period technology stock, its net-supply vector is
\[
\bar{\mathbf s}
=
\left(
-a,\,
-\ell,\,
-c_r,\,
a,\,
a\left(1+\bar\alpha\frac{\ell}{c_r}\right)
\right)^\top
\]
The first three components are demands for current technology stock, labor, and the research scale claim, while the last two components are supplies of current technology service and next-period technology stock. The current technology stock is thus used both to provide current productive services and as the base for future technology accumulation.
Let \(p_a^{(t)}\), \(w^{(t)}\), \(p_r^{(t)}\), \(p_v^{(t)}\), and \(p_a^{(t+1)}\) denote the prices of current technology stock, labor, research scale claim, current technology service, and next-period technology stock, respectively. The corresponding explicit marginal-pricing conditions are
\[
w^{(t)}
=
p_a^{(t+1)}
\bar\alpha
\frac{a}{c_r}
\]
\[
p_a^{(t)}
=
p_v^{(t)}
+
p_a^{(t+1)}
\left(
1+\bar\alpha\frac{\ell}{c_r}
\right)
\]
and
\[
p_r^{(t)}
=
-
p_a^{(t+1)}
\bar\alpha
\frac{a\ell}{c_r^2}
\]
Although the R&D firm is associated with five commodities, only three marginal-pricing conditions are required because its independent decision variables are the three inputs \(a\), \(\ell\), and \(c_r\); the two outputs are determined by these inputs through the R&D technology.
The first condition equates the wage to the marginal value generated by an additional unit of R&D labor. The second decomposes the value of the current technology stock into the value of its current technology service and its contribution to the next-period technology stock. The third determines the price of the research scale claim associated with the degree-one homogenization. In the implementation, \(\ell\) is also used as the activity level of the R&D firm, so the reported R&D activity levels directly represent equilibrium R&D labor inputs.
The representative consumer supplies the dated labor endowments, the initial technology stock, and the scale-claim commodities, and demands the dated products. Since the consumer side is unchanged from the underlying intertemporal model, no additional behavioral specification is required for the multiplicative R&D mechanism.
Finally, there is no useful R&D activity in period \(n_p-1\), because technology generated in that period would become available only as \(\alpha^{(n_p)}\) and could not be used by any production activity within the finite horizon. A terminal technology agent is therefore introduced to convert the remaining technology stock into the technology service required by the final production firm. This terminal agent is a computational transfer device rather than an additional behavioral type of economic agent.


Numerical Equilibrium
The GEMB implementation described above can be illustrated with \(n_p=20\), \(\rho=0.7\), \(\alpha^{(1)}=1\), \(\bar\alpha=0.005\), and \(\omega=100\). For these parameters,
\[
\bar\alpha\omega=0.5>\frac{1}{\rho}-1
\]
so the corresponding infinite-horizon model has positive R&D. For the finite-horizon model, the analytical solution gives \(k^*=6\), implying that the last period with positive R&D is
\[
n_p-k^*-1=13
\]
Thus R&D is positive in periods \(1,\ldots,13\) and zero thereafter. Productivity increases through \(\alpha^{(14)}\) and then remains constant.
The numerical equilibrium obtained with GEMB reproduces these analytical results. In particular, the equilibrium R&D labor inputs coincide with the finite-horizon solution, and the resulting productivity path follows the corresponding technology-accumulation path. This provides a numerical verification of both the analytical solution and the GEMB representation of the multiplicative R&D technology.



Listing 3: A \(6\times3\) Technology-Accumulation Intertemporal Equilibrium Model with Linear Multiplicative R&D


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEMB
import GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEM

np = 20

rho = 0.7
alpha1 = 1.0
alpha_bar = 0.005
omega = 100.0

np >= 3 || throw(ArgumentError("np must be at least 3."))

product(t) = CommodityRef(:product; period=t)
labor(t) = CommodityRef(:labor; period=t)
technology_stock(t) = CommodityRef(:technology_stock; period=t)
technology_service(t) = CommodityRef(:technology_service; period=t)
product_scale_claim(t) = CommodityRef(:product_scale_claim; period=t)
research_scale_claim(t) = CommodityRef(:research_scale_claim; period=t)

quantity_start = 100.0
research_start = 10.0

product_p0 =
    rho .^ (0:(np - 2))

labor_p0 =
    alpha1 .* product_p0

technology_service_p0 =
    quantity_start .* product_p0

technology_stock_p0 =
    copy(technology_service_p0)

for t in (np - 2):-1:1
    technology_stock_p0[t] =
        technology_service_p0[t] +
        (1 + alpha_bar * research_start) *
        technology_stock_p0[t + 1]
end

product_scale_claim_p0 =
    -quantity_start .* product_p0

research_scale_claim_p0 =
    -research_start .* alpha_bar .* technology_stock_p0[2:end]

p0 = vcat(
    product_p0,
    labor_p0,
    technology_stock_p0,
    technology_service_p0,
    product_scale_claim_p0,
    research_scale_claim_p0,
)

production_function =
    v -> v[1] * v[2] / v[3]

marginal_product_function = v -> begin
    a, x, cs = v
    [x * cs, a * cs, -a * x]
end

production_spec = ProductionFunctionSpec(
    production_function,
    marginal_product_function;
    behavior=:stationary,
)

research_net_supply = function (
    variables,
    prices,
    observed_values=Any[],
)
    ell, a, cs = variables
    [
        -a,
        -ell,
        -cs,
        a,
        a * (1 + alpha_bar * ell / cs),
    ]
end

research_conditions = function (
    variables,
    prices,
    net_supply,
)
    ell, a, cs = variables
    p_stock,
    wage,
    p_claim,
    p_service,
    p_next_stock = prices

    [
        wage -
        p_next_stock * alpha_bar * a / cs,

        p_stock -
        p_service -
        p_next_stock *
        (1 + alpha_bar * ell / cs),

        p_claim +
        p_next_stock *
        alpha_bar * a * ell / cs^2,
    ]
end

model = GEMBModel(
    [
        CommoditySpec(
            :product;
            axes=(period=2:np,),
            price_lower_bound=0.0,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :labor;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=0.0,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :technology_stock;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=0.0,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :technology_service;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=0.0,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :product_scale_claim;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=-Inf,
        ),
        CommoditySpec(
            :research_scale_claim;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 2),),
            price_lower_bound=-Inf,
        ),
    ];
    numeraire=product(2),
)

for t in 1:(np - 1)
    add_agent!(
        model,
        production_spec;
        outputs=product(t + 1),
        demands=[
            technology_service(t),
            labor(t),
            product_scale_claim(t),
        ],
        activity_start=quantity_start,
        demand_start=[
            alpha1,
            quantity_start,
            1.0,
        ],
        demand_lower_bounds=fill(1.0e-12, 3),
        production_multiplier_start=product_p0[t],
        name=Symbol("production_$t"),
    )
end

for t in 1:(np - 2)
    add_net_supply_agent!(
        model,
        research_net_supply;
        commodities=[
            technology_stock(t),
            labor(t),
            research_scale_claim(t),
            technology_service(t),
            technology_stock(t + 1),
        ],
        variable_names=[
            :activity,
            :technology_input,
            :scale_claim,
        ],
        variable_lower_bounds=[
            0.0,
            1.0e-12,
            1.0e-12,
        ],
        variable_upper_bounds=[
            omega,
            Inf,
            Inf,
        ],
        variable_start=[
            research_start,
            alpha1,
            1.0,
        ],
        condition_rule=
            GEM.ExplicitAgentConditions(
                research_conditions,
            ),
        name=Symbol("research_$t"),
    )
end

add_agent!(
    model,
    ActivityDemandSpec(
        (activity, prices) -> [activity],
    );
    outputs=technology_service(np - 1),
    demands=technology_stock(np - 1),
    activity_start=alpha1,
    activity_lower_bound=0.0,
    name=:terminal_technology,
)

add_agent!(
    model,
    CESMarginalUtilitySpec(
        rho .^ (2:np);
        es=1.0,
    );
    demands=[CommodityRef(:product)],
    endowments=[
        CommodityRef(:labor),
        technology_stock(1),
        CommodityRef(:product_scale_claim),
        CommodityRef(:research_scale_claim),
    ],
    endowment_quantities=vcat(
        fill(omega, np - 1),
        [alpha1],
        fill(1.0, np - 1),
        fill(1.0, np - 2),
    ),
    demand_start=fill(quantity_start, np - 1),
    demand_lower_bounds=fill(1.0e-12, np - 1),
    multiplier_start=
        rho^2 / quantity_start,
    multiplier_lower_bound=0.0,
    name=:consumer,
)

result = solve(
    model;
    p0=p0,
    residual_tol=1.0e-9,
    silent=true,
)

result.solved || error("Equilibrium solve failed.")

stats = equilibrium_statistics(model, result)

print_equilibrium_statistics(
    model,
    result;
    show_matrices=false,
)

research_labor =
    stats.activity_levels[np:(2 * np - 3)]

alpha_path =
    alpha1 .* cumprod(
        1 .+ alpha_bar .* research_labor,
    )

title: Intertemporal Equilibrium with Knowledge Production
text:
Exponential Multiplicative R&D
Consider an alternative multiplicative R&D specification,
\[
\alpha^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha^{(t)}
e^{\bar\alpha\ell^{(t)}}
\]
where \(\ell^{(t)}\) denotes R&D labor in period \(t\). As before, production in period \(t\) generates the product available in period \(t+1\), so useful R&D activities occur only in periods \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-2\).
For the infinite-horizon model, positive R&D occurs when
\[
\bar\alpha\omega
>
\frac{1}{\rho}-1
\]
and the corresponding R&D labor input is
\[
\ell^*
=
\omega
-
\frac{1-\rho}{\rho\bar\alpha}
\]
When R&D is positive, productivity follows
\[
\alpha^{(t)}
=
\alpha^{(1)}
\left(
e^{\bar\alpha\omega-\frac{1-\rho}{\rho}}
\right)^{t-1},
\qquad
t=1,2,\ldots
\]
For the finite-horizon model, the optimal R&D labor input is
\[
\ell^{*(t)}
=
\begin{cases}
0,
&
\displaystyle
\bar\alpha\omega
\leq
\frac{1-\rho}
{\rho\left(1-\rho^{n_p-t-1}\right)}
\\[1em]
\displaystyle
\omega
-
\frac{1-\rho}
{\rho\bar\alpha\left(1-\rho^{n_p-t-1}\right)},
&
\displaystyle
\bar\alpha\omega
>
\frac{1-\rho}
{\rho\left(1-\rho^{n_p-t-1}\right)}
\end{cases},
\qquad
t=1,\ldots,n_p-2
\]
When the long-run R&D condition holds, define
\[
k^*
=
\left\lfloor
\frac{
\ln\left(
1-\frac{1-\rho}{\rho\bar\alpha\omega}
\right)
}{
\ln\rho
}
\right\rfloor
+1
\]
Provided that \(n_p\geq k^*+2\), the last period with positive R&D is \(n_p-k^*-1\). The resulting productivity level \(\alpha^{(n_p-k^*)}\) is then maintained throughout the remaining periods.

title: Finite-Horizon Canonical Dynamic Macroeconomic Equilibrium
text:
Assume the following (see Torres, 2016, chap. 2):

The economy has \(n_p\) periods and \(n_p-1\) production intervals. A product firm operating in period \(t\) starts production at the beginning of the period and obtains its output at the end of period \(t\), or equivalently at the beginning of period \(t+1\). Commodities dated at different periods are treated as different commodities.
The economy contains three types of dated commodities: products, labor, and capital rentals. Product firms and capital-rental firms operate in periods \(t=1,\ldots,n_p-1\), and there is one intertemporal consumer. The product also serves as capital.
The product firm operating in period \(t\) rents capital \(k^{(t)}\) and employs labor \(x^{(t)}\) to produce the product available in period \(t+1\) according to

\[
y^{(t+1)}
=
\alpha^{(t)}
\left(k^{(t)}\right)^{\beta_1}
\left(x^{(t)}\right)^{1-\beta_1}
\]
where \(\beta_1=0.35\) and \(\alpha^{(t)}=1\) in the benchmark case.

The capital-rental firm purchases the current product as capital, supplies its use to the product firm, and carries the undepreciated capital into the next period. Thus, an activity level of \(k^{(t)}\) requires \(k^{(t)}\) units of \(\mathrm{product}^{(t)}\) and supplies \(k^{(t)}\) units of \(\mathrm{capital_rental}^{(t)}\) together with \((1-\delta)k^{(t)}\) units of \(\mathrm{product}^{(t+1)}\), where \(\delta=0.06\). Combining the two production activities, the total product supply generated in period \(t\) and available in period \(t+1\) is \(y^{(t+1)}+(1-\delta)k^{(t)}\).
The representative consumer initially owns \(k^{(1)}=286.6341\) units of product and is endowed with \(\omega=100\) units of labor in each production period. title: Finite-Horizon Canonical Dynamic Macroeconomic Equilibrium
text:
Equilibrium with Tail Adjustment
To mitigate the finite-horizon tail effect, an additional demand for the terminal product is introduced alongside the ordinary single-period utility components. Let \(\eta>0\) denote its endogenous weight. The intertemporal utility structure is
\[
U
\sim
\prod_{t=1}^{n_p-1}
\left(u^{(t)}\right)^{\varGamma^{t-1}}
\left(c^{(n_p)}\right)^\eta
\]
The ordinary single-period preferences and discount factors remain unchanged. When the nested Cobb–Douglas utility is represented by a single CESSpec, the weight on the terminal product becomes \(\beta_2\varGamma^{n_p-2}+\eta\).
Since capital is the state variable of the model, \(\eta\) is paired with the tail condition
\[
k^{(n_p-2)}
=
k^{(n_p-1)}
\]
Thus, the terminal weight is determined endogenously so that the last two capital stocks coincide.
With \(n_p=20\), the steady-state benchmark is approximately
\[
k^*=286.6,
\qquad
x^*=36.04,
\qquad
y^*=74.47,
\qquad
c^*=57.27
\]
The tail-adjusted equilibrium gives
\[
\eta=1.157,
\qquad
\frac{\eta}{\varGamma^{18}}
\approx2.002
\]
where \(\varGamma^{18}\) is the discount weight on the last ordinary single-period utility component. The last two capital stocks are
\[
k^{(18)}
=
k^{(19)}
=
286.6
\]



Listing 2: A \(3\times3\) Canonical Dynamic Macroeconomic Equilibrium Model with Tail Adjustment


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling

np = 20

discount_factor = 0.97
depreciation_rate = 0.06
capital_share = 0.35
consumption_share = 0.4

labor_endowment = 100.0
initial_capital = 286.6341

technology = ones(np - 1)

product(t) = GEMB.CommodityRef(:product; period=t)
labor(t) = GEMB.CommodityRef(:labor; period=t)
capital_rental(t) = GEMB.CommodityRef(:capital_rental; period=t)

intertemporal_weights = discount_factor .^ (0:(np - 2))

model = GEMB.GEMBModel(
    [
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :product;
            axes=(period=1:np,),
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-10,
        ),
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :labor;
            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),

        ),

            axes=(period=1:(np - 1),),
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-10,
        ),
    ];

)

rental_spec = GEMB.ActivityDemandSpec(
    (activity, prices) -> [activity],
)

for t in 1:(np - 1)
    GEMB.add_agent!(
        model,
        GEMB.CESSpec(
            [capital_share, 1 - capital_share];
            es=1.0,
            alpha=technology[t],
        );
        outputs=product(t + 1),
        demands=[
            capital_rental(t),
            labor(t),
        ],
        activity_start=100.0,
        name=Symbol("firm_$t"),
    )

    GEMB.add_agent!(
        model,
        rental_spec;
        outputs=[
            capital_rental(t),
            product(t + 1),
        ],
        output_coefficients=[
            1.0,
            1 - depreciation_rate,
        ],
        demands=product(t),
        activity_start=100.0,
        name=Symbol("rental_$t"),
    )
end

    [product(t) for t in 1:np],
    [labor(t) for t in 1:(np - 1)],
)

consumer_net_supply = function (
    local_variables,
    local_prices,
    observed_values=Any[],
)
    terminal_weight = local_variables[1]

    product_prices = local_prices[1:np]
    labor_prices = local_prices[(np + 1):(2 * np - 1)]

    product_weights =
        consumption_share .* intertemporal_weights
    product_weights[end] += terminal_weight

    labor_weights =
        (1 - consumption_share) .* intertemporal_weights

    beta = vcat(product_weights, labor_weights)
    beta ./= sum(beta)

    income =
        product_prices[1] * initial_capital +
        labor_endowment * sum(labor_prices)

    demand_prices = vcat(
        product_prices[2:np],
        labor_prices,
    )

    demand = GEMB.CES_demand(
        beta,
        income,
        demand_prices;
        es=1.0,
    )

    T = promote_type(
        eltype(local_variables),
        eltype(local_prices),
    )
    supply = zeros(T, 2 * np - 1)

    supply[1] = initial_capital
    supply[2:np] .= -demand[1:(np - 1)]
    supply[(np + 1):(2 * np - 1)] .=
        labor_endowment .- demand[np:(2 * np - 2)]

    return supply
end

tail_condition = function (
    local_variables,
    local_prices,
    net_supply,
    observed_values,
)
    return [observed_values[1] - observed_values[2]]
end

GEMB.add_net_supply_agent!(
    model,
    consumer_net_supply;
    commodities=consumer_commodities,
    variable_names=[:terminal_weight],
    variable_lower_bounds=[1.0e-8],
    variable_upper_bounds=[Inf],
    variable_start=[1.0],

            :activity,
        ),
        GEM.AgentVariableRef(
            Symbol("rental_$(np - 1)"),
            :activity,

    ],
    condition_rule=GEM.ExplicitAgentConditions(
        tail_condition,
    ),
    name=:consumer,
)

target_mpk =
    gross_return - (1 - depreciation_rate)

capital_labor_ratio =
    (capital_share / target_mpk)^(1 / (1 - capital_share))

steady_mpl =
    (1 - capital_share) *
    capital_labor_ratio^capital_share

product_price_1 =
    1 / (discount_factor * steady_mpl)

product_p0 =
    product_price_1 .* discount_factor .^ (0:(np - 1))

labor_p0 =
    discount_factor .^ (0:(np - 2))

rental_p0 =
    product_p0[1:(np - 1)] .-
    (1 - depreciation_rate) .* product_p0[2:np]

p0 = vcat(
    product_p0,
    labor_p0,
    rental_p0,
)

result = GEMB.solve(
    model;
    p0=p0,
    residual_tol=1.0e-9,
    silent=true,
)

result.solved || error("Equilibrium solve failed.")

prices = result.prices

product_prices = prices[1:np]
labor_prices = prices[(np + 1):(2 * np - 1)]
rental_prices = prices[(2 * np):(3 * np - 2)]

new_output = [
    result.agent_variable_values[2 * t - 1][1]
    for t in 1:(np - 1)
]

capital = [
    result.agent_variable_values[2 * t][1]
    for t in 1:(np - 1)
]

labor_input = [
    -result.agent_net_supplies[2 * t - 1][3]
    for t in 1:(np - 1)
]

consumer_supply = result.agent_net_supplies[end]

product_demand =
    -consumer_supply[2:np]

labor_supply =
    consumer_supply[(np + 1):(2 * np - 1)]

leisure =
    labor_endowment .- labor_supply

terminal_weight =
    result.agent_variable_values[end][1]

ordinary_last_weight =
    consumption_share * intertemporal_weights[end]

ordinary_consumption = copy(product_demand)
ordinary_consumption[end] *=
    ordinary_last_weight /
    (ordinary_last_weight + terminal_weight)

terminal_product_demand =
    product_demand[end] - ordinary_consumption[end]

total_output =
    new_output .+
    (1 - depreciation_rate) .* capital

println()
println("Canonical dynamic macroeconomic equilibrium")
println("-------------------------------------------")
println("Solved: ", result.solved)
println("Terminal weight:       ", terminal_weight)
println(
    "Terminal weight ratio: ",
    terminal_weight / intertemporal_weights[end],
)
println(
    "Last-capital difference: ",
    capital[end - 1] - capital[end],
)

println()
println("Equilibrium paths")
println("Capital:              ", capital)
println("Labor input:          ", labor_input)
println("New output:           ", new_output)
println("Ordinary consumption: ", ordinary_consumption)
println("Terminal demand:       ", terminal_product_demand)
println("Leisure:              ", leisure)

title: Minimum-Wage and Endogenous Labor Supply
text:

The economy contains three commodities and two economic agents, a firm and a consumer. The commodities are product, labor, and land. The product is taken as the numeraire commodity.
The firm uses labor and land to produce the product according to the constant-returns-to-scale production function
\[
y=\alpha l^\beta t^{1-\beta},
\qquad
\alpha>0,\quad0<\beta<1
\]
where \(l\) and \(t\) denote labor and land inputs, respectively.
The consumer supplies labor and land and demands only the product. Its product demand is denoted by \(c\). The land supply \(\bar t>0\) is exogenous, whereas the labor supply \(s\geq0\) is endogenous.
Assume that labor is abundant and that the minimum wage is binding. The minimum wage may be legally mandated or determined by the subsistence level. In the model, the labor price is fixed exogenously at the minimum wage \(\bar w>0\), and the endogenous labor supply \(s\) adjusts so that the labor market clears at this fixed wage. In other words, only part of the available labor enters the market, while the remainder stays outside the market.

Let the price vector be
\[
\mathbf p=(1,w,r)^\top
\]
where \(w\) and \(r\) are the prices of labor and land, respectively. Given \(y\), \(c\), \(s\), \(w\), and \(r\), the demand and supply matrices can be written explicitly as
\[
\mathbf D(y,c,w,r)=
\begin{bmatrix}
0&
c\\[6pt]
\frac{y}{\alpha}
\left(
\frac{\beta r}{(1-\beta)w}
\right)^{1-\beta}
&
0\\[10pt]
\frac{y}{\alpha}
\left(
\frac{(1-\beta)w}{\beta r}
\right)^\beta
&
0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
\mathbf S(y,s)=
\begin{bmatrix}
y&0\\
0&s\\
0&\bar t
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The wide-sense structural equilibrium model is
\[
\begin{cases}
\mathbf p^\top\mathbf D(y,w,r)=\mathbf p^\top\mathbf S(y)\\
\mathbf D(y,w,r)\mathbf 1=\mathbf S(y)\mathbf 1\\
w=\bar w
\end{cases}
\]
where the third equation imposes the binding minimum-wage condition.

title: Minimum-Wage and Endogenous Labor Supply
text:
Assume the following:

The economy contains three commodities and two economic agents, a firm and a consumer. The commodities are product, labor, and land. The product is taken as the numeraire commodity.
The firm uses labor and land to produce the product according to the constant-returns-to-scale production function
\[
y=\alpha l^\beta t^{1-\beta},
\qquad
\alpha>0,\quad0<\beta<1
\]
where \(l\) and \(t\) denote labor and land inputs, respectively.
The consumer supplies labor and land and demands only the product. Its product demand is denoted by \(c\). The land supply \(\bar t>0\) is exogenous, whereas the labor supply \(s\geq0\) is endogenous.

\[

\begin{bmatrix}
0&
c\\[6pt]
\frac{y}{\alpha}
\left(
\frac{\beta r}{(1-\beta)w}
\right)^{1-\beta}
&
0\\[10pt]
\frac{y}{\alpha}
\left(

\right)^\beta
&
0

and

title: Minimum-Wage and Endogenous Labor Supply
text:
Equilibrium
The equilibrium labor supply is
\[
s^*
=
\bar t
\left(
\frac{\alpha\beta}{\bar w}
\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\beta}}
\]
and the corresponding equilibrium land price, output, and consumption are
\[
r^*
=
\alpha(1-\beta)
(s^*)^\beta\bar t^{-\beta}
\]
\[
y^*
=
\alpha(s^*)^\beta\bar t^{1-\beta}
\]
and
\[
c^*=y^*
\]
For the numerical example, let
\[
\alpha=2,
\qquad
\beta=0.5,
\qquad
\bar t=100,
\qquad
\bar w=2
\]
The equilibrium price vector is
\[
\mathbf p^*=(1,2,0.5)^\top
\]
and the equilibrium quantities are
\[
s^*=l^*=25,
\qquad
t^*=100,
\qquad
y^*=c^*=100
\]
Accordingly, the equilibrium demand and supply matrices are
\[
\mathbf D^*=
\begin{bmatrix}
0&100\\
25&0\\
100&0
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf S^*=
\begin{bmatrix}
100&0\\
0&25\\
0&100
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Thus, fixing the labor price at \(\bar w=2\) endogenously determines the equilibrium labor supply as \(s^*=25\).
The corresponding GEMB implementation is given in Listing Listing 1. The endogenous labor supply is represented by a condition variable paired with the fixed-wage condition. The consumer is represented by an ActivityDemandSpec: its activity level determines product consumption, while a customized output specification supplies the endogenous quantity of labor and the fixed quantity of land.



Listing 1: A \(3\times2\) Equilibrium Model with a Fixed Wage and Endogenous Labor Supply


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEM
using GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEMB
import GeneralEquilibriumModeling.GEMB: activity_supply

alpha = 2.0
beta = 0.5
land_supply = 100.0
fixed_wage = 2.0

struct LaborLandSupplySpec <: AbstractActivitySupplySpec
    land_supply::Float64
end

function activity_supply(
    spec::LaborLandSupplySpec,
    activity,
    prices,
    observed_values,
)
    labor_supply = observed_values[1]
    [labor_supply, spec.land_supply]
end

model = GEMBModel(
    [
        :product,
        CommoditySpec(:labor; price_lower_bound=1.0e-6),
        CommoditySpec(:land; price_lower_bound=1.0e-6),
    ];
    numeraire=:product,
    numeraire_value=1.0,
)

add_agent!(
    model,
    ConditionAgentSpec(
        (variables, observed_values) -> [
            observed_values[1] - fixed_wage,
        ],
    );
    variable_names=:labor_supply,
    variable_start=100.0,
    variable_lower_bounds=0.0,
    variable_upper_bounds=Inf,
    observed_variables=[
        PriceVariableRef(:labor),
    ],
    name=:labor_condition,
)

add_agent!(
    model,
    CESSpec(
        [beta, 1.0 - beta];
        es=1.0,
        alpha=alpha,
    );
    outputs=:product,
    demands=[:labor, :land],
    activity_start=100.0,
    name=:firm,
)

add_agent!(
    model,
    ActivityDemandSpec(
        (activity, prices) -> [activity],
    );
    outputs=[:labor, :land],
    output_spec=LaborLandSupplySpec(land_supply),
    demands=:product,
    activity_start=100.0,
    observed_variables=[
        agent_variable_ref(:labor_condition, :labor_supply),
    ],
    condition_rule=TotalRevenueExpenditureBalanceConditions(),
    name=:consumer,
)

result = solve(
    model;
    p0=[1.0, 1.0, 1.0],
    residual_tol=1.0e-10,
    silent=true,
)

labor_supply = result.agent_variable_values[1][1]
firm_output = result.agent_variable_values[2][1]
consumer_consumption = result.agent_variable_values[3][1]

println("Solved: ", result.solved)
println("Prices [product, labor, land]: ", result.prices)
println("Labor supply: ", labor_supply)
println("Firm output: ", firm_output)
println("Consumer consumption: ", consumer_consumption)
println("Total net supply: ", result.total_net_supply)

title: Excess Burden of a Commodity Tax under Quasilinear Utility Functions
text:
This example is essentially a pure exchange economy, with a tax intermediary added to implement the commodity tax.
Assume the following:

The economy contains four commodities: corn, iron, taxed iron, and tax certificates; and four economic agents: consumer 1, consumer 2, a firm, and the government. Corn is taken as the numeraire commodity.
Consumer 1 has the utility function
\[
u_1(x_1,x_3)
=
x_1+\beta_1\left(\alpha_1x_3-\frac12x_3^2\right)
\]
where \(x_1\) denotes corn, \(x_3\) denotes taxed iron, and \(\alpha_1,\beta_1>0\). Consumer 1 is endowed with \(\omega_1\) units of corn.
Consumer 2 has the utility function
\[
u_2(x_1,x_2)
=
x_1+\beta_2\left(\alpha_2x_2-\frac12x_2^2\right)
\]
where \(x_1\) denotes corn, \(x_2\) denotes iron, and \(\alpha_2,\beta_2>0\). Consumer 2 is endowed with \(\omega_2\) units of iron. Consumer 1 wishes to purchase iron supplied by consumer 2, and the government imposes a commodity tax on iron.
The firm acts as a tax agency. It uses iron and tax certificates as inputs to produce taxed iron. Under the tax system, consumer 1 must purchase taxed iron from the firm, while consumer 2 must sell iron through the firm.
The government is endowed with one unit of the tax certificate and has the utility function \(u_G=x_1\).

title: Excess Burden of a Commodity Tax under Quasilinear Utility Functions
text:
Equilibrium
Suppose the parameter values ensure interior solutions in both the taxed and no-tax equilibria, with positive consumption of corn and iron-related commodities for both consumers and positive equilibrium prices for \(\tau>0\). Consumer 1’s demand for taxed iron is
\[
x_3(p_3)
=
\alpha_1-\frac{p_3}{\beta_1}
\]
and consumer 2’s demand for iron is
\[
x_2(p_2)
=
\alpha_2-\frac{p_2}{\beta_2}
\]
Let the price vector be
\[
\mathbf p:=(1,p_2,p_3,p_4)^\top
\]
where \(p_2\) is the price of iron, \(p_3\) is the price of taxed iron, and \(p_4\) is the price of the tax certificate. Let \(y\) denote the firm’s activity level, which is also its output of taxed iron; let \(\mathbf w=(w_1,w_2)^\top\) denote the vector of consumer incomes; let \(u\) denote the government’s utility level; and let \(\tau>0\) denote the ad valorem commodity tax rate.
Consumer 1 purchases \(x_3\) units of taxed iron, so its demand for corn is \(w_1-p_3x_3\). Consumer 2 consumes \(x_2\) units of iron and sells the remaining iron, so its demand for corn is \(w_2-p_2x_2\).
To produce one unit of taxed iron, the firm uses one unit of iron and tax certificates with a total value equal to \(\tau p_2\). Therefore, producing \(y\) units of taxed iron requires
\[
\frac{yp_2\tau}{p_4}
\]
units of tax certificates.
The government sells its endowment of tax certificates and spends the resulting income entirely on corn.
The demand matrix is therefore
\[
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,u,\mathbf w,y)
:=
\begin{bmatrix}
w_1-p_3x_3 & w_2-p_2x_2 & 0 & u\\
0 & x_2 & y & 0\\
x_3 & 0 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 0 & \frac{yp_2\tau}{p_4} & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and the supply matrix is
\[
\mathbf S(y)
:=
\begin{bmatrix}
\omega_1 & 0 & 0 & 0\\
0 & \omega_2 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 0 & y & 0\\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Solving the equality-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model gives
\[
p_2^*
=
\frac{
\beta_1\beta_2(\alpha_1+\alpha_2-\omega_2)
}{
\beta_1+(1+\tau)\beta_2
}
\]
\[
p_3^*
=
(1+\tau)p_2^*
\]
and
\[
p_4^*
=
y^*p_2^*\tau
\]
The equilibrium quantity of taxed iron is
\[
y^*
=
\alpha_1-\frac{p_3^*}{\beta_1}
\]
with
\[
x_3^*=y^*
\]
and
\[
x_2^*
=
\alpha_2-\frac{p_2^*}{\beta_2}
\]
The equilibrium consumer incomes and government utility level are
\[
w_1^*=\omega_1
\]
\[
w_2^*=p_2^*\omega_2
\]
and
\[
u^*=p_4^*
\]
respectively.
The commodity tax generates a wedge between the buyer’s price and the seller’s price:
\[
p_3^*-p_2^*
=
\tau p_2^*
\]
Consider the parameter values
\[
\beta_1=\beta_2=0.05,\qquad
\alpha_1=120,\qquad
\alpha_2=100
\]
\[
\omega_1=1000,\qquad
\omega_2=100,\qquad
\tau=1
\]
The analytical solution is
\[
p_2^*=2,\qquad
p_3^*=4,\qquad
p_4^*=80
\]
and
\[
y^*=40
\]
Hence the equilibrium price vector is
\[
\mathbf p^*
=
(1,2,4,80)^\top
\]
Consumer 1 consumes 840 units of corn and 40 units of taxed iron. Consumer 2 consumes 80 units of corn and 60 units of iron. The government consumes 80 units of corn.

title: Excess Burden of a Commodity Tax under Quasilinear Utility Functions
section: Excess Burden of the Commodity Tax
text:
Excess Burden of the Commodity Tax
The equilibrium utilities of the two consumers under the commodity tax rate \(\tau\) are
\[
u_1^*(\tau)
=
\omega_1-p_3^*x_3^*
+
\beta_1
\left(
\alpha_1x_3^*
-\frac12(x_3^*)^2
\right)
\]
and
\[
u_2^*(\tau)
=
p_2^*(\omega_2-x_2^*)
+
\beta_2
\left(
\alpha_2x_2^*
-\frac12(x_2^*)^2
\right)
\]
The government’s equilibrium utility is
\[
u_G^*(\tau)
=
u^*
=
p_4^*
=
y^*p_2^*\tau
\]
Since the three utility functions are normalized in units of corn, define the utilitarian social welfare measure under the commodity tax rate \(\tau\) as
\[
W(\tau)
:=
u_1^*(\tau)
+
u_2^*(\tau)
+
u_G^*(\tau)
\]
Let \(W(0)\) denote social welfare in the no-tax equilibrium. The excess burden of the commodity tax is
\[
W(0)-W(\tau)
\]
which can be calculated as
\[
W(0)-W(\tau)
=
\frac{
\beta_1^2\beta_2^2\tau^2
(\alpha_1+\alpha_2-\omega_2)^2
}{
2(\beta_1+\beta_2)
\left[\beta_1+\beta_2(1+\tau)\right]^2
}
\]
Using the equilibrium price \(p_2^*\), this can be written more simply as
\[
W(0)-W(\tau)
=
\frac{(\tau p_2^*)^2}
{2(\beta_1+\beta_2)}
\]
The reduction in the equilibrium quantity of traded iron relative to the no-tax equilibrium is
\[
y^*(0)-y^*(\tau)
=
\frac{\tau p_2^*}{\beta_1+\beta_2}
\]
while the commodity-tax wedge is
\[
p_3^*-p_2^*
=
\tau p_2^*
\]
Hence the excess burden can also be expressed as
\[
W(0)-W(\tau)
=
\frac12
(p_3^*-p_2^*)
\left[y^*(0)-y^*(\tau)\right]
\]
which is the area of the excess-burden triangle generated by the commodity tax.
For the numerical parameter values above, the no-tax equilibrium quantity is
\[
y^*(0)=60
\]
while the equilibrium quantity under \(\tau=1\) is
\[
y^*(1)=40
\]
The commodity-tax wedge is
\[
p_3^*-p_2^*=2
\]
and therefore the excess burden is
\[
\frac12(60-40)(4-2)=20
\]
Equivalently,
\[
W(0)=1430,\qquad
W(1)=1410
\]
so that
\[
W(0)-W(1)=20
\]
When \(\tau=0\), the tax certificate has no economic role and its equilibrium price is zero, while the term \(\frac{yp_2\tau}{p_4}\) in the demand matrix becomes indeterminate. The no-tax equilibrium should therefore be represented without the tax-certificate commodity, or equivalently interpreted through the limit as \(\tau\to0^+\) when welfare is considered.
The corresponding GEMB implementation is given in Listing 1.



Listing 1: A \(4\times4\) General Equilibrium Model with a Commodity Tax and Quasilinear Utility Functions


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling

beta1 = 0.05
beta2 = 0.05
alpha1 = 120.0
alpha2 = 100.0

omega1 = 1000.0
omega2 = 100.0

tau = 1.0

consumer1_demand = (income, p) -> begin
    p1, p3 = p
    x3 = alpha1 - p3 / (beta1 * p1)
    x1 = (income - p3 * x3) / p1
    [x1, x3]
end

consumer2_demand = (income, p) -> begin
    p1, p2 = p
    x2 = alpha2 - p2 / (beta2 * p1)
    x1 = (income - p2 * x2) / p1
    [x1, x2]
end

model = GEMB.GEMBModel(
    [
        :corn,
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :iron;
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-8,
        ),
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :taxed_iron;
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-8,
        ),
        GEMB.CommoditySpec(
            :tax_certificate;
            price_lower_bound=1.0e-8,
        ),
    ];
    numeraire=:corn,
    numeraire_value=1.0,
)

GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    GEMB.MarshallDemandConsumerSpec(consumer1_demand);
    demands=[:corn, :taxed_iron],
    endowments=:corn,
    endowment_quantities=omega1,
    name=:consumer1,
)

GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    GEMB.MarshallDemandConsumerSpec(consumer2_demand);
    demands=[:corn, :iron],
    endowments=:iron,
    endowment_quantities=omega2,
    name=:consumer2,
)

GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    GEMB.CESSpec(
        [1.0];
        es=0.0,
        alpha=1.0,
    );
    outputs=:taxed_iron,
    demands=:iron,
    claim_rate=tau,
    claim=GEMB.CommodityRef(:tax_certificate),
    activity_start=100.0,
    name=:tax_agency,
)

GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    GEMB.CESSpec(
        [1.0];
        es=0.0,
        alpha=1.0,
    );
    demands=:corn,
    endowments=:tax_certificate,
    endowment_quantities=1.0,
    activity_start=100.0,
    name=:government,
)

result = GEMB.solve(
    model;
    p0=[1.0, 1.5, 3.0, 60.0],
    residual_tol=1.0e-10,
    silent=true,
)

stats = GEMB.equilibrium_statistics(model, result)

GEMB.print_equilibrium_statistics(model, result)

title: Introduction
text:
The book GeneralEquilibriumModeling.jl and Structural Equilibrium Models presents a collection of basic applied general equilibrium models together with numerical solution programs based on GeneralEquilibriumModeling.jl.

title: Introduction
text:
Introduction to Structural Equilibrium Models
The strict-sense structural equilibrium model extends the input and output coefficient matrices of the von Neumann equilibrium model to unit demand and unit supply matrices that may depend on prices, utility levels, and activity levels (Li, 2019, chap. 3). After incorporating any discount factor into the unit supply matrix, it can be written as
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf p^{\top}\mathbf A(\cdot)
&\geq
\mathbf p^{\top}\mathbf B(\cdot)\\
\mathbf A(\cdot)\mathbf z
&\leq
\mathbf B(\cdot)\mathbf z
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\mathbf p\geq\mathbf 0\) is the price vector and \(\mathbf z\geq\mathbf 0\) is the activity-level vector. The first condition represents unit revenue-expenditure balance, and the second represents supply-demand balance (i.e., market clearing).
The mixed-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model is written directly in terms of the demand and supply matrices of economic agents:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf p^{\top}\mathbf D(\cdot)
&=
\mathbf p^{\top}\mathbf S(\cdot)\\
\mathbf D(\cdot)\mathbf 1
&\leq
\mathbf S(\cdot)\mathbf 1
\end{aligned}
\]
The first condition represents total revenue-expenditure balance for each economic agent, while the second states that aggregate demand for each commodity does not exceed aggregate supply.
If no commodity is in excess supply at equilibrium, the model becomes the equality-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf p^{\top}\mathbf D(\cdot)
&=
\mathbf p^{\top}\mathbf S(\cdot)\\
\mathbf D(\cdot)\mathbf 1
&=
\mathbf S(\cdot)\mathbf 1
\end{aligned}
\]
Here, every economic agent satisfies total revenue-expenditure balance, and supply equals demand for every commodity.

For details, see The von Neumann Equilibrium Model and Structural Equilibrium Models.

title: Monopolistic Supply
text:
Assume the following (see Li, 2019, p. 146):

The economy contains two commodities and two consumers. Commodity 2 is the numeraire commodity, so the price vector is
\[
\mathbf p=(p_1,1)^\top
\]
Consumer 1 is endowed with \(s_1>0\) units of commodity 1, while consumer 2 is endowed with \(s_2>0\) units of commodity 2. The endowment matrix is

\[
\mathbf S=
\begin{bmatrix}
s_1&0\\
0&s_2
\end{bmatrix}
\]

The two consumers have the same reduced-form CES utility function
\[
u(x_1,x_2)
=
(x_1^{-1}+x_2^{-1})^{-1}
\]
In the competitive benchmark, both consumers supply their full endowments. In the monopoly case, consumer 1 may choose to supply only \(q\) units of commodity 1, where \(0<q\leq s_1\), while the remaining \(s_1-q\) units are left idle. The production process and the consumption of final products are omitted in this simplified model. Accordingly, the CES utility function is a reduced-form representation of the utility generated through the omitted production and final-product consumption process, while the two commodities themselves represent production factors. Consumer 2 continues to supply its full endowment.

For the above utility function, the demand matrix can be written as
\[
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,\mathbf u)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
u_1\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{p_1}}\right)
&
u_2\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{p_1}}\right)
\\
u_1(1+\sqrt{p_1})
&
u_2(1+\sqrt{p_1})
\end{bmatrix}
\]

title: Monopolistic Supply
text:
Assume the following (see Li, 2019, p. 146):

The economy contains two commodities and two consumers. Commodity 2 is the numeraire commodity, so the price vector is
\[
\mathbf p=(p_1,1)^\top
\]
Consumer 1 is endowed with \(s_1>0\) units of commodity 1, while consumer 2 is endowed with \(s_2>0\) units of commodity 2. The endowment matrix is

\[
\mathbf S=
\begin{bmatrix}
s_1&0\\
0&s_2
\end{bmatrix}
\]

The two consumers have the same reduced-form CES utility function
\[
u(x_1,x_2)
=
(x_1^{-1}+x_2^{-1})^{-1}
\]
In the competitive benchmark, both consumers supply their full endowments. In the monopoly case, consumer 1 may choose to supply only \(q\) units of commodity 1, where \(0<q\leq s_1\), while the remaining \(s_1-q\) units are left idle. The production process and the consumption of final products are omitted in this simplified model. Accordingly, the CES utility function is a reduced-form representation of the utility generated through the omitted production and final-product consumption process, while the two commodities themselves represent production factors. Consumer 2 continues to supply its full endowment.

For the above utility function, the demand matrix can be written as
\[
\mathbf D(\mathbf p,\mathbf u)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
u_1\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{p_1}}\right)
&
u_2\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{p_1}}\right)
\\
u_1(1+\sqrt{p_1})
&
u_2(1+\sqrt{p_1})
\end{bmatrix}
\]

title: Monopolistic Supply
text:
Analytical Solution
Under full endowment supply, solving the equality-form wide-sense structural equilibrium model gives
\[
\mathbf p^*
=
\left(
\left(\frac{s_2}{s_1}\right)^2,
1
\right)^\top
\]
and
\[
u_1^*
=
\frac{s_1s_2^2}{(s_1+s_2)^2},
\qquad
u_2^*
=
\frac{s_2s_1^2}{(s_1+s_2)^2}
\]
For fixed \(s_2\), consumer 1’s equilibrium utility satisfies
\[
\frac{d u_1^*}{d s_1}
=
\frac{s_2^2(s_2-s_1)}{(s_1+s_2)^3}
\]
Hence \(u_1^*\) increases with \(s_1\) when \(s_1<s_2\), decreases with \(s_1\) when \(s_1>s_2\), and reaches its maximum at \(s_1=s_2\).
For any given supply level \(q\) chosen by consumer 1, where \(0<q\leq s_1\), the resulting competitive equilibrium is obtained by replacing \(s_1\) with \(q\). Thus,
\[
p_1(q)
=
\left(\frac{s_2}{q}\right)^2
\]
and consumer 1’s equilibrium utility is
\[
u_1(q)
=
\frac{q s_2^2}{(q+s_2)^2}
\]
The monopoly supply problem is therefore
\[
\max_{0<q\leq s_1}u_1(q)
\]
Since
\[
\frac{d u_1}{dq}
=
\frac{s_2^2(s_2-q)}{(q+s_2)^3}
\]
the optimal supply is
\[
q^*
=
\min\{s_1,s_2\}
\]
In particular, if \(s_1>s_2\),
\[
q^*=s_2<s_1
\]
so consumer 1 increases its equilibrium utility by withholding part of its endowment from the market.
For example, let
\[
s_1=200,
\qquad
s_2=100
\]
Under full supply, the competitive equilibrium is
\[
\mathbf p^*=(0.25,1)^\top
\]
with
\[
u_1^*=22.2222,
\qquad
u_2^*=44.4444
\]
The monopoly solution is
\[
q^*=100
\]
which gives
\[
\mathbf p^*=(1,1)^\top
\]
and
\[
u_1^*=u_2^*=25
\]
Consumer 1 therefore raises its equilibrium utility from approximately \(22.2222\) to \(25\) by reducing its supply from \(200\) to \(100\).

title: Monopolistic Supply
text:
Numerical Solution
The numerical solution treats the monopoly problem as a hierarchical equilibrium problem. For each candidate supply \(q\), the inner problem constructs the corresponding pure-exchange economy and solves its competitive equilibrium with GEMB. The resulting equilibrium utility of consumer 1 is then returned to the outer optimization problem. The numerical procedure can be summarized as
\[
q
\longrightarrow
\text{competitive equilibrium}
\longrightarrow
\mathbf p^*(q),\mathbf u^*(q)
\longrightarrow
u_1^*(q)
\longrightarrow
\max_q u_1^*(q)
\]
With \(s_1=200\) and \(s_2=100\), the numerical solution gives
\[
q^*\approx100,
\qquad
\mathbf p^*\approx(1,1)^\top
\]
and
\[
u_1^*\approx25,
\qquad
u_2^*\approx25
\]
which agrees with the analytical solution.



Listing 1: A \(2\times2\) Pure-Exchange Monopoly Model with Hierarchical Equilibrium


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling
using Optim

s1 = 200.0
s2 = 100.0

# u(x1, x2) = (x1^(-1) + x2^(-1))^(-1)
const preference = GEMB.CESSpec(
    [1.0, 1.0];
    es=0.5,
)

function solve_competitive_equilibrium(q, s2)
    model = GEMB.GEMBModel(
        [
            GEMB.CommoditySpec(
                :commodity_1;
                price_lower_bound=1.0e-8,
            ),
            :commodity_2,
        ];
        numeraire=:commodity_2,
    )

    GEMB.add_agent!(
        model,
        preference;
        demands=[:commodity_1, :commodity_2],
        endowments=:commodity_1,
        endowment_quantities=q,
        activity_start=100.0,
        name=:consumer_1,
    )

    GEMB.add_agent!(
        model,
        preference;
        demands=[:commodity_1, :commodity_2],
        endowments=:commodity_2,
        endowment_quantities=s2,
        activity_start=100.0,
        name=:consumer_2,
    )

    result = GEMB.solve(
        model;
        silent=true,
    )

    u1 = result.agent_variable_values[1][1]
    u2 = result.agent_variable_values[2][1]

    return (
        model=model,
        result=result,
        u1=u1,
        u2=u2,
    )
end

function monopoly_objective(q)
    equilibrium = solve_competitive_equilibrium(q, s2)
    return -equilibrium.u1
end

# Prevent inner equilibrium breakdown at q = 0
q_lower = 0.01 * s1

optimization = optimize(
    monopoly_objective,
    q_lower,
    s1,
    Brent();
    rel_tol=1.0e-8,
    abs_tol=1.0e-8,
)

q_star = Optim.minimizer(optimization)

baseline = solve_competitive_equilibrium(s1, s2)
monopoly = solve_competitive_equilibrium(q_star, s2)

println("========== Baseline competitive equilibrium ==========")
println("Supply of consumer 1 = ", s1)
println("Prices = ", baseline.result.prices)
println("Utility of consumer 1 = ", baseline.u1)
println("Utility of consumer 2 = ", baseline.u2)

println("\n========== Monopoly equilibrium ==========")
println("Optimal supply of consumer 1 = ", q_star)
println("Prices = ", monopoly.result.prices)
println("Utility of consumer 1 = ", monopoly.u1)
println("Utility of consumer 2 = ", monopoly.u2)
println("Outer optimization converged = ", Optim.converged(optimization))

GEMB.print_equilibrium_statistics(
    monopoly.model,
    monopoly.result,
)

title: General Equilibrium and Linear Programming
text:
Assume the following:

The economy contains four commodities and four economic agents. The commodities are one product and three primary factors, while the economic agents are three firms and one consumer. The product is taken as the numeraire commodity.
Each firm uses the three primary factors to produce the product with fixed input and output coefficients. The unit demand and supply matrices are
\[
\mathbf A(u)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0&0&0&u\\
8&6&1&0\\
4&2&1.5&0\\
2&1.5&0.5&0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
\mathbf B
=
\begin{bmatrix}
60&30&20&0\\
0&0&0&48\\
0&0&0&20\\
0&0&0&8
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The consumer demands only the product. Its utility level \(u\) is equal to the quantity of the product consumed. Hence maximizing utility is equivalent to maximizing total product output.
The consumer supplies \(48\), \(20\), and \(8\) units of the three primary factors, respectively.

Let
\[
\mathbf p=(1,p_2,p_3,p_4)^\top
\]
be the price vector and
\[
\mathbf z=(z_1,z_2,z_3,1)^\top
\]
the activity-level vector, where \(z_1,z_2,z_3\) are the activity levels of the three firms and the consumer population is normalized to one.
The equilibrium can be represented by the structural equilibrium model
\[
\mathbf p^\top\mathbf A(u)
\geq
\mathbf p^\top\mathbf B
\] \[
\mathbf A(u)\mathbf z
\leq
\mathbf B\mathbf z
\]
The equilibrium is
\[
(z_1^*,z_2^*,z_3^*)
=
(2,0,8)
\]
with
\[
u^*=280
\]
and the equilibrium price vector is
\[
\mathbf p^*
=
(1,0,10,10)^\top
\]

title: General Equilibrium and Linear Programming
section: Primal and Dual Linear Programming Problems
text:
Primal and Dual Linear Programming Problems
The structural equilibrium model above simultaneously characterizes the solutions to the primal and dual linear programming problems corresponding to the Dakota Furniture Company example in Winston (2003). Define
\[
\mathbf z_f=(z_1,z_2,z_3)^\top,
\qquad
\mathbf b=(60,30,20)^\top,
\qquad
\mathbf e=(48,20,8)^\top
\]
and the input-coefficient matrix
\[
\mathbf A_f
=
\begin{bmatrix}
8&6&1\\
4&2&1.5\\
2&1.5&0.5
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The primal linear programming problem is
\[
\max_{\mathbf z_f\geq\mathbf0}
\mathbf b^\top\mathbf z_f
\qquad
\text{s.t.}
\qquad
\mathbf A_f\mathbf z_f\leq\mathbf e
\]
Its dual problem is
\[
\min_{\mathbf p_f\geq\mathbf0}
\mathbf p_f^\top\mathbf e
\qquad
\text{s.t.}
\qquad
\mathbf p_f^\top\mathbf A_f\geq\mathbf b^\top
\]
where
\[
\mathbf p_f=(p_2,p_3,p_4)^\top
\]
is the vector of primary-factor prices, with the product price normalized to one.
The equilibrium firm activity levels
\[
\mathbf z_f^*=(2,0,8)^\top
\]
solve the primal problem, while the equilibrium factor prices
\[
\mathbf p_f^*=(0,10,10)^\top
\]
solve the dual problem. The optimal values of the two problems are equal:
\[
\mathbf b^\top\mathbf z_f^*
=
\mathbf p_f^{*\top}\mathbf e
=
280
\]
Thus, solving the structural equilibrium model simultaneously solves the primal allocation problem and the dual pricing problem.
In the GEMB numerical representation, the consumer population is not represented by a separate activity variable. Instead, the consumer’s activity level represents its utility level. The resulting activity levels are therefore
\[
(2,0,8,280)
\]
for the three firms and the consumer, respectively.



Listing 1: A \(4\times4\) General Equilibrium Representation of a Linear Programming Problem


using GeneralEquilibriumModeling

input_coefficients = [
    8.0  6.0  1.0
    4.0  2.0  1.5
    2.0  1.5  0.5
]

output_coefficients = [60.0, 30.0, 20.0]
factor_endowments = [48.0, 20.0, 8.0]
factors = [:factor_1, :factor_2, :factor_3]

model = GEMB.GEMBModel(
    [:product, factors...];
    numeraire=:product,
)

for j in 1:3
    coefficients = input_coefficients[:, j]

    production = GEMB.ActivityDemandSpec(
        (z, p) -> z .* coefficients,
    )

    GEMB.add_agent!(
        model,
        production;
        outputs=:product,
        output_coefficients=output_coefficients[j],
        demands=factors,
        activity_start=100.0,
        name=Symbol("firm_", j),
    )
end

consumer = GEMB.ActivityDemandSpec(
    (u, p) -> [u],
)

GEMB.add_agent!(
    model,
    consumer;
    demands=:product,
    endowments=factors,
    endowment_quantities=factor_endowments,
    activity_start=100.0,
    name=:consumer,
)

result = GEMB.solve(
    model;
    silent=true,
)

GEMB.print_equilibrium_statistics(model, result)
